title: Section 4
context: A university lecturer is giving a talk on how traditional and modern housing designs adapt to different climates.

audio.t: You will hear a lecturer talking about climate-adaptive housing.
Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to look at how architects design homes that work with the climate rather than against it.
Long before air conditioning existed, builders around the world had already solved many of these problems, so let's begin with traditional, or vernacular, architecture.
In hot, dry regions, the classic solution is thick walls made from adobe, which is simply sun-dried earth mixed with straw.
The walls absorb heat slowly during the day and release it at night, so the temperature inside stays surprisingly stable.
Many of those houses are also built around a central courtyard, and the narrow streets between them are designed to give shade for most of the day.
Now, people sometimes think the secret is the colour of the walls, but in fact it's the thermal mass, meaning the sheer thickness of the material.
Moving to the tropics, we find a very different problem, which is humidity rather than heat.
Here, houses are often raised on stilts. This allows airflow beneath the floor, which keeps the rooms dry and cool, and it also protects against small floods.
The roofs are usually steep as well, but not because of snow, as students often assume. They're designed to shed heavy rain quickly.
Of course, in some places flooding is so serious that raising the house a metre or two is not enough.
One modern response is the amphibious house. It looks like an ordinary home, but it sits on a hollow concrete pontoon.
When the river rises, the whole building floats upwards along steel posts, and it settles back down again when the water falls.
Let's now turn to cold climates, where the priority is capturing and keeping warmth.
In the northern hemisphere, architects place the largest windows facing south, because that's where the winter sun is strongest.
I should point out that I'm sometimes asked about east-facing windows, but these only get weak morning sun, so they're less useful.
Of course, windows lose heat as well as gain it, so modern designs combine triple glazing with thick insulation to cut heat loss to a minimum.
Now, what about cities? Concrete and asphalt absorb heat, which makes city centres much warmer than the surrounding countryside.
This is known as the urban heat island effect, and one popular way to reduce it is the green roof, which is a roof covered in plants.
Green roofs cool the air through evaporation, they absorb rainwater, and they also provide a habitat for insects and birds.
A common objection is cost. Many people think it's cheaper to demolish an old house and build a new one.
But a recent study of retrofitting, meaning adapting existing buildings, found that it cost on average 40 per cent less than rebuilding.
The original estimate in the draft report was 30 per cent, but that figure was revised after the researchers included the cost of removing waste.
Finally, let's look briefly at the future. A number of research teams are developing homes that adjust themselves automatically.
For instance, sensors measure the sunlight and temperature, and then they control self-adjusting shutters on the windows.
The shutters close at midday to keep the house cool, and open again in the evening to let the heat out.
To sum up, good climate design is not about expensive technology, but about understanding the local environment.
For next week, please read the two articles on the reading list, and think about which climate you would find most challenging to design for.

blocks.instructions: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.q: In hot, dry regions, homes have thick ______ walls that release heat slowly at night.
questions.explain: "thick walls made from adobe, which is simply sun-dried earth mixed with straw" - bẫy: màu tường không phải yếu tố chính.

questions.q: Courtyards and narrow streets are designed to provide ______.
questions.explain: "the narrow streets between them are designed to give shade for most of the day".

questions.q: Houses on stilts in the tropics allow ______ beneath the floor.
questions.explain: "This allows airflow beneath the floor, which keeps the rooms dry and cool".

questions.q: Steep roofs in the tropics are designed to shed ______ quickly.
questions.explain: Không phải tuyết như sinh viên hay nghĩ: "They're designed to shed heavy rain quickly."

questions.q: An amphibious house sits on a hollow concrete ______.
questions.explain: "it sits on a hollow concrete pontoon" và nổi lên theo cột thép khi nước dâng.

questions.q: In cold northern regions, the largest windows face ______.
questions.explain: "architects place the largest windows facing south"; hướng đông chỉ có nắng sớm yếu nên bị loại.

questions.q: Triple glazing and thick insulation reduce ______.
questions.explain: "combine triple glazing with thick insulation to cut heat loss to a minimum".

questions.q: Green roofs help to reduce the urban ______ effect.
questions.explain: "This is known as the urban heat island effect, and one popular way to reduce it is the green roof".

questions.q: Retrofitting existing buildings costs on average ______ per cent less than rebuilding.
questions.explain: Số liệu nháp là 30% nhưng đã được chỉnh lại: "it cost on average 40 per cent less than rebuilding".

questions.q: Future homes may use sensors to control self-adjusting ______ on windows.
questions.explain: "sensors measure the sunlight and temperature, and then they control self-adjusting shutters on the windows".
